**Ulysses S. Grant** (born **Hiram Ulysses Grant**;[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-3) April 27, 1822–July 23, 1885) was the 18th [president of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States"), serving from 1869 to 1877, and was the [Commanding General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commanding_General_of_the_United_States_Army "Commanding General of the United States Army") of the [Union Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Army "Union Army"), leading it to victory in the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War") in 1865.

Grant was born in Ohio and graduated from the [United States Military Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Military_Academy "United States Military Academy") in 1843. He served with distinction in the [Mexican–American War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexican%E2%80%93American_War "Mexican–American War"), but returned to civilian life impoverished in 1854. In 1861, shortly after the Civil War began, Grant joined the Union Army. He rose to prominence after securing victories in the [western theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_theater_of_the_American_Civil_War "Western theater of the American Civil War") in 1862. In 1863, he led the [Vicksburg campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicksburg_campaign "Vicksburg campaign") that gave Union forces control of the [Mississippi River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River "Mississippi River") and dealt a major strategic blow to the Confederacy. President [Abraham Lincoln](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Lincoln "Abraham Lincoln") promoted Grant to [lieutenant general](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lieutenant_general_(United_States) "Lieutenant general (United States)") and command of all Union armies after [his victory at Chattanooga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chattanooga_campaign "Chattanooga campaign"). Grant fought [Robert E. Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Lee "Robert E. Lee") through the [Overland Campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overland_Campaign "Overland Campaign"), which ended when Lee surrendered to Grant [at Appomattox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Appomattox_Court_House#Surrender "Battle of Appomattox Court House"). In 1866, President [Andrew Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Johnson "Andrew Johnson") promoted Grant to [General of the Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_of_the_Army_(United_States)#Post%E2%80%93American_Civil_War_era "General of the Army (United States)"). Grant broke with Johnson over [Reconstruction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconstruction_era "Reconstruction era") policies. A war hero, drawn in by his sense of duty, Grant was unanimously nominated by the [Republican Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") and [elected president in 1868](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1868_United_States_presidential_election "1868 United States presidential election").

As president, Grant stabilized the post-war economy, supported Reconstruction and [the Fifteenth Amendment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fifteenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution "Fifteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution"), and prosecuted the [Ku Klux Klan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ku_Klux_Klan "Ku Klux Klan"). An effective civil rights executive, Grant signed a bill to create the [United States Department of Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Justice "United States Department of Justice") and worked with [Radical Republicans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radical_Republicans "Radical Republicans") to protect African Americans. In 1871, he created the [first Civil Service Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Civil_Service_Commission "United States Civil Service Commission"). Grant was re-elected in [the 1872 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1872_United_States_presidential_election "1872 United States presidential election"), but was inundated by executive scandals during his second term. His response to the [Panic of 1873](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panic_of_1873 "Panic of 1873") was ineffective in halting the [Long Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Depression "Long Depression"), which contributed to the [Democrats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)")[winning the House majority in 1874](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1874%E2%80%9375_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections "1874–75 United States House of Representatives elections"). Grant's Native American policy was to assimilate Indians into Anglo-American culture. In his foreign policy, the [_Alabama_ Claims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabama_Claims "Alabama Claims") against Britain were peacefully resolved, but the Senate rejected his proposal to [annex Santo Domingo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proposed_United_States_annexation_of_Santo_Domingo "Proposed United States annexation of Santo Domingo"). During the [disputed 1876 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1876_United_States_presidential_election "1876 United States presidential election"), he facilitated the approval by Congress of a compromise.

Leaving office in 1877, Grant undertook [a world tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_tour_of_Ulysses_S._Grant "World tour of Ulysses S. Grant"), becoming the first president to circumnavigate the world. In 1880, he [was unsuccessful in obtaining the Republican nomination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1880_Republican_National_Convention "1880 Republican National Convention") for a third term. In 1885, dying of throat cancer, Grant wrote [his memoirs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_Memoirs_of_U._S._Grant "Personal Memoirs of U. S. Grant"), which were posthumously published and became a major critical and financial success. At his death, he was the most popular American and was memorialized as a symbol of national unity. Due to the [pseudohistorical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudohistory "Pseudohistory") and [negationist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_negationism "Historical negationism") mythology of the [Lost Cause of the Confederacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lost_Cause_of_the_Confederacy "Lost Cause of the Confederacy") spread by Confederate sympathizers around the turn of the 20th century, [historical assessments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_reputation_of_Ulysses_S._Grant "Historical reputation of Ulysses S. Grant") and [rankings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_rankings_of_presidents_of_the_United_States "Historical rankings of presidents of the United States") of Grant's presidency suffered considerably before they began recovering in the 21st century.

## Early life and education

Further information: [Early life and career of Ulysses S. Grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_life_and_career_of_Ulysses_S._Grant "Early life and career of Ulysses S. Grant")

[![Image 10: Color drawing of Grant's birthplace, a simple one-story structure, with fence and trees in front, next to the Ohio River with steamboat passing by](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/45/Birthplace_of_Ulysses_S_Grant%2C_color_illustration%2C_cropped.jpg/250px-Birthplace_of_Ulysses_S_Grant%2C_color_illustration%2C_cropped.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Birthplace_of_Ulysses_S_Grant,_color_illustration,_cropped.jpg)

[Grant's birthplace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grant's_birthplace "Grant's birthplace") in [Point Pleasant, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_Ohio "Point Pleasant, Ohio")

Grant's father, [Jesse Root Grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesse_Root_Grant "Jesse Root Grant"), was a [Whig Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whig_Party_(United_States) "Whig Party (United States)") supporter and a fervent abolitionist.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHesseltine20014-4) He and [Hannah Simpson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannah_Simpson "Hannah Simpson") were married on June 24, 1821, and their first child, Hiram Ulysses Grant, was born on April 27, 1822.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely19815%E2%80%936White20168%E2%80%939-5) To honor his father-in-law, Jesse named the boy "Hiram Ulysses", though he always referred to him as "Ulysses".[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimpson20142%E2%80%933White20169%E2%80%9310-6) In 1823, the family moved to [Georgetown, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgetown,_Ohio "Georgetown, Ohio"), where five siblings were born: Simpson, Clara, Orvil, Jennie, and Mary.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTELongacre20066%E2%80%937-7) At the age of five, Ulysses started at a [subscription school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subscription_school "Subscription school") and later attended two private schools.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981497White201616,_18-8) In the winter of 1836–1837, Grant was a student at [Maysville Seminary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Brett_Richeson_House#Maysville_Academy "John Brett Richeson House"), and in the autumn of 1838, he attended [John Rankin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Rankin_(abolitionist) "John Rankin (abolitionist)")'s academy.

In his youth, Grant developed an unusual ability to ride and manage horses;[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely19818,_10,_140%E2%80%93141White201621-9) his father gave him work driving supply wagons and transporting people.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012a8White201619-10) Unlike his siblings, Grant was not required to attend church by his [Methodist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodist "Methodist") parents.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTELongacre20066%E2%80%937Waugh200914-11) For the rest of his life, he prayed privately and never officially joined any denomination.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimpson20142%E2%80%933Longacre20066%E2%80%937-12) To others, including his own son, Grant appeared to be [agnostic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agnostic "Agnostic").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWaugh200914-13) Grant was largely apolitical before the war but wrote, "If I had ever had any political sympathies they would have been with the [Whigs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whig_Party_(United_States) "Whig Party (United States)"). I was raised in that school."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow201799%E2%80%93100-14)

## Early military career and personal life

### West Point and first assignment

[![Image 11: Engraving of a young Grant in uniform](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5a/Ulysses_Grant_at_21.jpg/250px-Ulysses_Grant_at_21.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ulysses_Grant_at_21.jpg)

Grant as a young officer, c. 1845–1847

At Jesse Grant's request, Representative [Thomas L. Hamer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_L._Hamer "Thomas L. Hamer") nominated Ulysses to the [United States Military Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Military_Academy "United States Military Academy") at [West Point, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Point,_New_York "West Point, New York"), in spring 1839. Grant was accepted on July 1.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite201624%E2%80%9325-15) Unfamiliar with Grant, Hamer altered his name, so Grant was enlisted under the name "U. S. Grant".[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-19)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198112Smith200124,_83Simon19673%E2%80%934Kahan20182-20) Since the initials "U.S." also stood for "[Uncle Sam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncle_Sam "Uncle Sam")", he became known among army colleagues as "Sam."[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite201630-21)

Initially, Grant was indifferent to military life, but within a year he reexamined his desire to leave the academy and later wrote that "on the whole I like this place very much".[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimpson201413%E2%80%9314Smith200126%E2%80%9328-22) He earned a reputation as the ["most proficient" horseman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horsemanship_of_Ulysses_S._Grant "Horsemanship of Ulysses S. Grant").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198110-23) Seeking relief from military routine, he studied under [Romantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanticism "Romanticism") artist [Robert Walter Weir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Walter_Weir "Robert Walter Weir"), producing nine surviving artworks.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith200127McFeely198116%E2%80%9317-24) He spent more time reading books from the library than his academic texts.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198116%E2%80%9317Smith200126%E2%80%9327-25) On Sundays, cadets were required to march to services at the academy's church, which Grant disliked.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite201641-26) Quiet by nature, he established a few intimate friends among fellow cadets, including [Frederick Tracy Dent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Tracy_Dent "Frederick Tracy Dent") and [James Longstreet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Longstreet "James Longstreet"). He was inspired both by the Commandant, Captain [Charles Ferguson Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Ferguson_Smith "Charles Ferguson Smith"), and by General [Winfield Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winfield_Scott "Winfield Scott"), who visited the academy to review the cadets. Grant later wrote of the military life, "there is much to dislike, but more to like."[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012a12%E2%80%9313-27)

Grant graduated on June 30, 1843, ranked 21st out of 39 in his class and was promoted the next day to [brevet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brevet_(military) "Brevet (military)")[second lieutenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_lieutenant "Second lieutenant").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow201727Longacre200621Cullum1850256%E2%80%93257-28) He planned to resign his commission after his four-year term. He would later write that among the happiest days of his life were the day he left the presidency and the day he left the academy.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow201728McFeely198116,_19-29) Despite his excellent horsemanship, he was not assigned to the cavalry, but to the [4th Infantry Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4th_Infantry_Regiment_(United_States) "4th Infantry Regiment (United States)").[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-31) Grant's first assignment was the [Jefferson Barracks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_Barracks "Jefferson Barracks") near [St. Louis, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis,_Missouri "St. Louis, Missouri").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith200128%E2%80%9329Brands2012a15Chernow201781-32) Commanded by Colonel [Stephen W. Kearny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_W._Kearny "Stephen W. Kearny"), this was the nation's largest military base in the West.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith200128%E2%80%9329-33) Grant was happy with his commander but looked forward to the end of his military service and a possible teaching career.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith200130%E2%80%9333-34)

### Marriage and family

In 1844, Grant accompanied Frederick Dent to Missouri and met his family, including Dent's sister [Julia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julia_Grant "Julia Grant"). The two soon became engaged.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith200130%E2%80%9333-34) On August 22, 1848, they were married at Julia's home in St. Louis. Grant's abolitionist father disapproved of the Dents' owning slaves, and neither of Grant's parents attended the wedding.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow201761%E2%80%9362White2016102Waugh200933-35) Grant was flanked by three fellow West Point graduates in their blue uniforms, including Longstreet, Julia's cousin.[[e]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-38)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith200173%E2%80%9374Waugh200933Chernow201762White2016102-39)

The couple had four children: [Frederick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Dent_Grant "Frederick Dent Grant"), [Ulysses Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant_Jr. "Ulysses S. Grant Jr.") ("Buck"), [Ellen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nellie_Grant "Nellie Grant") ("Nellie"), and [Jesse II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesse_Root_Grant_(politician) "Jesse Root Grant (politician)").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith200173-40) After the wedding, Grant obtained a two-month extension to his leave and returned to St. Louis, where he decided that, with a wife to support, he would remain in the army.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimpson201449-41)

### Mexican–American War

Main article: [Mexican–American War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexican%E2%80%93American_War "Mexican–American War")

[![Image 12: An American depiction of the Battle of Monterrey within the city](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e7/Battle_of_Monterrey.jpg/250px-Battle_of_Monterrey.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Battle_of_Monterrey.jpg)

The [Battle of Monterrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Monterrey "Battle of Monterrey") during which Grant saw military action

Grant's unit was stationed in Louisiana as part of the [Army of Occupation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Army_of_Occupation_(Mexico) "Army of Occupation (Mexico)") under Major General [Zachary Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zachary_Taylor "Zachary Taylor").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith200135%E2%80%9337Brands2012a15%E2%80%9317-42) In September 1846, President [James K. Polk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_K._Polk "James K. Polk") ordered Taylor to march 150 miles (240 km) south to the [Rio Grande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_Grande "Rio Grande"). Marching to [Fort Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Texas "Fort Texas"), to prevent a Mexican siege, Grant experienced combat for the first time on May 8, 1846, at the [Battle of Palo Alto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Palo_Alto "Battle of Palo Alto").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198130%E2%80%9331Brands2012a23-43) Grant served as regimental quartermaster, but yearned for a combat role; when finally allowed, he led a charge at the [Battle of Resaca de la Palma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Resaca_de_la_Palma "Battle of Resaca de la Palma").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite201680-44) He demonstrated his equestrian ability at the [Battle of Monterrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Monterrey "Battle of Monterrey") by volunteering to carry a dispatch past snipers; he hung off the side of his horse, keeping the animal between him and the enemy.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198133%E2%80%9334Brands2012a37-45) Polk, wary of Taylor's growing popularity, divided his forces, sending some troops (including Grant's unit) to form a new army under Major General [Winfield Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winfield_Scott "Winfield Scott").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198134%E2%80%9335-46)

Traveling by sea, Scott's army landed at [Veracruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veracruz "Veracruz") and advanced toward [Mexico City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico_City "Mexico City").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012a41%E2%80%9342-47) They met the Mexican forces at the battles of [Molino del Rey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Molino_del_Rey "Battle of Molino del Rey") and [Chapultepec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Chapultepec "Battle of Chapultepec").[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198136-48) For his bravery at Molino del Rey, Grant was brevetted first lieutenant on September 30.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite201666Encyclopedia_of_the_Mexican-American_War_2013271-49) At San Cosmé, Grant directed his men to drag a disassembled [mountain howitzer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M1841_mountain_howitzer "M1841 mountain howitzer") into a church steeple, then reassembled it and bombarded nearby Mexican troops.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198136-48) His bravery and initiative earned him his brevet promotion to captain.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimpson201444Encyclopedia_of_the_Mexican-American_War_2013271-50) On September 14, 1847, Scott's army marched into the city; Mexico [ceded the vast territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Guadalupe_Hidalgo "Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo"), including [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), to the U.S. on February 2, 1848.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith200167%E2%80%9368,_70,_73Brands2012a49%E2%80%9352-51) During the war, Grant established a commendable record as a daring and competent soldier and began to consider a career in the army.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite201675-52)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEncyclopedia_of_the_Mexican-American_War_2013271-53) He studied the tactics and strategies of Scott and Taylor and emerged as a seasoned officer, writing in his memoirs that this is how he learned much about military leadership.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimpson2014458Chernow201758-54) In retrospect, although he respected Scott, he identified his own leadership style with Taylor's. Grant later believed the Mexican war was morally unjust and that the territorial gains were designed to expand slavery. He opined that the Civil War was divine punishment for U.S. aggression against Mexico.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198130%E2%80%9331,_37%E2%80%9338-55)

Historians have pointed to the importance of Grant's experience as an assistant quartermaster during the war. Although he was initially averse to the position, it prepared Grant in understanding military supply routes, transportation systems, and logistics, particularly with regard to "provisioning a large, mobile army operating in hostile territory", according to biographer Ronald White.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite201680-44) Grant came to recognize how wars could be won or lost by factors beyond the battlefield.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite201685,_96Chernow201746-56)

### Post-war assignments and resignation

Grant's first post-war assignments took him and Julia to [Detroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit "Detroit") on November 17, 1848. He was soon transferred to [Madison Barracks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madison_Barracks "Madison Barracks"), a desolate outpost in upstate New York in need of supplies and repair. After four months, Grant was sent back to his quartermaster job in Detroit.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow201765-57) When the discovery of [gold in California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Gold_Rush "California Gold Rush") brought prospectors and settlers to the territory, Grant and the 4th infantry were ordered to reinforce the small garrison there. Grant was charged with bringing the soldiers and a few hundred civilians from New York City to Panama, [overland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maritime_history_of_California#To_California_via_Panama "Maritime history of California") to the Pacific and then north to California. Julia, eight months pregnant with Ulysses Jr., did not accompany him.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith200176%E2%80%9378Chernow201773%E2%80%9374-58)

While Grant was in Panama, a [cholera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cholera "Cholera") epidemic killed many soldiers and civilians. Grant organized a field hospital in [Panama City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama_City "Panama City"), and moved the worst cases to a hospital barge offshore.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow201774-59) When orderlies protested having to attend to the sick, Grant did much of the nursing himself, earning high praise from observers.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith200176%E2%80%9378Chernow201773%E2%80%9374-58) In August, Grant arrived in San Francisco. His next assignment sent him north to [Vancouver Barracks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vancouver_Barracks "Vancouver Barracks") in the [Oregon Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oregon_Territory "Oregon Territory").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith200178Chernow201775-60)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-61)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-62)

Grant tried several business ventures but failed, and in one instance his business partner absconded with $800 of Grant's investment, equivalent to $24,000 in 2024.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981Chernow2017-63) After he witnessed white agents cheating [local Indians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Pacific_Northwest_Coast "Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest Coast") of their supplies, and their devastation from [smallpox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smallpox "Smallpox") and [measles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measles "Measles") spread by white settlers, he developed empathy for their plight.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016487Chernow201778-64)

Promoted to [captain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_(U.S._Army) "Captain (U.S. Army)") on August 5, 1853, Grant was assigned to command Company F, [4th Infantry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4th_Infantry_Regiment_(United_States) "4th Infantry Regiment (United States)"), at the newly constructed [Fort Humboldt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Humboldt_State_Historic_Park "Fort Humboldt State Historic Park") in California.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198152Cullum1891171Chernow201781-65) Grant arrived at Fort Humboldt on January 5, 1854, commanded by Lieutenant Colonel [Robert C. Buchanan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_C._Buchanan "Robert C. Buchanan").[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow201781%E2%80%9383-66) Separated from his family, Grant began to drink.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198155Chernow201784%E2%80%9385-67) Colonel Buchanan reprimanded Grant for one drinking episode and told Grant to "resign or reform." Grant told Buchanan he would "resign if I don't reform."[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow201785-68) On Sunday, Grant was found influenced by alcohol, but not incapacitated, at his company's paytable.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTECullum1891171Chernow201784%E2%80%9385-69) Keeping his pledge to Buchanan, Grant resigned, effective July 31, 1854.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTECullum1891171Chernow201785%E2%80%9386-70) Buchanan endorsed Grant's resignation but did not submit any report that verified the incident.[[f]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-76)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith200186%E2%80%9387White2016118%E2%80%93120McFeely198155-77) Grant did not face court-martial, and the War Department said: "Nothing stands against his good name."[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTELongacre200655%E2%80%9358-78) Grant said years later, "the vice of intemperance (drunkenness) had not a little to do with my decision to resign."[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith200187%E2%80%9388Lewis1991328%E2%80%93332-79) With no means of support, Grant returned to St. Louis and reunited with his family.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012a77%E2%80%9378-80)

## Civilian struggles, slavery, and politics

[![Image 13: A small log cabin](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/09/Hardscrabble.jpg/250px-Hardscrabble.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hardscrabble.jpg)

"Hardscrabble", the log house built by Grant in between wars

In 1854, aged 32, Grant entered civilian life without any money-making vocation to support his growing family. It was the beginning of seven years of financial struggles and instability.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow201795,_106Simon2002242McFeely198160%E2%80%9361Brands2012a94%E2%80%9396-81) Grant's father offered him a place in the [Galena, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galena,_Illinois "Galena, Illinois"), branch of the family's leather business, but demanded Julia and the children stay in Missouri, with the Dents, or with the Grants in Kentucky. Grant and Julia declined. For the next four years, Grant farmed with the help of Julia's slave, Dan, on his brother-in-law's property, _Wish-ton-wish_, near [St. Louis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis "St. Louis").[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198158%E2%80%9360White2016125-82) The farm was not successful and to earn a living he sold firewood on St. Louis street corners.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198161-83)

In 1856, the Grants moved to land on Julia's father's farm, and built a home called "Hardscrabble" on [Grant's Farm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grant's_Farm "Grant's Farm"); Julia described it as an "unattractive cabin".[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198158%E2%80%9360Chernow201794-84) Grant's family had little money, clothes, and furniture, but always had enough food.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012a96-85) During the [Panic of 1857](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panic_of_1857 "Panic of 1857"), which devastated Grant as it did many farmers, Grant pawned his gold watch to buy Christmas gifts.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016128-86) In 1858, Grant rented out Hardscrabble and moved his family to Julia's father's [850-acre plantation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant_National_Historic_Site "Ulysses S. Grant National Historic Site").[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198162Brands2012a86White2016128-87) That fall, after having [malaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaria "Malaria"), Grant gave up farming.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012aWhite2016-88) Fearing that electing a [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") president would lead to a civil war, he voted for [Democrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") James Buchanan in 1856. He had the same fear in 1860 and preferred Douglas, the Democrat. However, he did not vote in 1860 because he lacked the residency requirement in Galena.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012a95,_109%E2%80%93110-89)

In 1858, Grant acquired a [slave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_slavery_in_Missouri "History of slavery in Missouri") from his father-in-law, a thirty-five-year-old man named William Jones.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith200194%E2%80%9395White2016130-90) Although Grant was not an [abolitionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abolitionist "Abolitionist") at the time, he disliked slavery and could not bring himself to force an enslaved man to work.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012a86%E2%80%9387-91) In March 1859, Grant freed Jones by a [manumission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manumission "Manumission") deed, potentially worth at least $1,000 (equivalent to $36,000 in 2025).[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith200194%E2%80%9395McFeely198169White2016130-92)

Grant moved to St. Louis, taking on a partnership with Julia's cousin Harry Boggs working in the real estate business as a bill collector, again without success and at Julia's prompting ended the partnership.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198164Brands2012a89%E2%80%9390White2016129%E2%80%93131-93) In August, Grant applied for a position as county engineer. He had thirty-five recommendations, but Grant was passed over by the [Free Soil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Soil_Party "Free Soil Party") and Republican county commissioners because he was believed to share his father-in-law's Democratic sentiments.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016131Simon19694%E2%80%935-94)

In April 1860, Grant and his family moved north to Galena, accepting a position in his father's leather goods business, "Grant & Perkins", run by his younger brothers Simpson and Orvil. In a few months, Grant paid off his debts.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198165%E2%80%9366White2016133,_136-95) The family attended the local Methodist church and he soon established himself as a reputable citizen.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016135%E2%80%9337-96)

## Civil War

Main article: [Ulysses S. Grant and the American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant_and_the_American_Civil_War "Ulysses S. Grant and the American Civil War")

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/20/Portrait_of_General_Ulysses_S._Grant_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Portrait_of_General_Ulysses_S._Grant_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Portrait_of_General_Ulysses_S._Grant_(cropped).jpg)

Portrait of General Grant, c. 1861-1865

On April 12, 1861, the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War") began when Confederate troops [attacked Fort Sumter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Fort_Sumter "Battle of Fort Sumter") in [Charleston, South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charleston,_South_Carolina "Charleston, South Carolina").[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016140-97) The news came as a shock in Galena, and Grant shared his neighbors' concern about the war.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012a121-98) On April 15, Lincoln called for 75,000 volunteers.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith200199-99) The next day, Grant attended a mass meeting to assess the crisis and encourage recruitment, and a speech by his father's attorney, [John Aaron Rawlins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Aaron_Rawlins "John Aaron Rawlins"), stirred Grant's patriotism.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016140%E2%80%93143Brands2012a121%E2%80%93122McFeely198173Bonekemper201217Smith200199Chernow2017125-100) In an April 21 letter to his father, Grant wrote out his views on the upcoming conflict: "We have a government and laws and a flag, and they must all be sustained. There are but two parties now, Traitors and Patriots."[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012a123-101)

### Early commands

Further information: [Kentucky in the American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky_in_the_American_Civil_War "Kentucky in the American Civil War")

On April 18, Grant chaired a second recruitment meeting, but turned down a captain's position as commander of the newly formed militia company, hoping his experience would aid him to obtain a more senior rank.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012a122%E2%80%93123McFeely198180Bonekemper2012-102) His early efforts to be recommissioned were rejected by Major General [George B. McClellan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_B._McClellan "George B. McClellan") and Brigadier General [Nathaniel Lyon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathaniel_Lyon "Nathaniel Lyon"). On April 29, supported by Congressman [Elihu B. Washburne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elihu_B._Washburne "Elihu B. Washburne") of Illinois, Grant was appointed military aide to Governor [Richard Yates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Yates_(19th-century_politician) "Richard Yates (19th-century politician)") and mustered ten regiments into the [Illinois militia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois_militia "Illinois militia"). On June 14, again aided by Washburne, Grant was appointed colonel and put in charge of the [21st Illinois Volunteer Infantry Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/21st_Illinois_Volunteer_Infantry_Regiment "21st Illinois Volunteer Infantry Regiment");[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-103) he appointed [John A. Rawlins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_A._Rawlins "John A. Rawlins") as his [aide-de-camp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aide-de-camp "Aide-de-camp") and brought order and discipline to the regiment. Soon after, Grant and the 21st Regiment were transferred to Missouri to dislodge Confederate forces.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFlood200545%E2%80%9346Smith2001113Bonekemper201218%E2%80%9320-104)

On August 5, with Washburne's aid, Grant was appointed brigadier general of volunteers.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBonekemper201221-105) Major General [John C. Frémont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_C._Fr%C3%A9mont "John C. Frémont"), Union commander of the West, passed over senior generals and appointed Grant commander of the District of Southeastern Missouri.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001117%E2%80%9318Bonekemper201221-106) On September 2, Grant arrived at [Cairo, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairo,_Illinois "Cairo, Illinois"), assumed command by replacing Colonel [Richard J. Oglesby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_J._Oglesby "Richard J. Oglesby"), and set up his headquarters to plan a campaign down the Mississippi, and up the Tennessee and Cumberland rivers.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016159Bonekemper201221-107)

After the Confederates moved into western Kentucky, taking Columbus, with designs on southern Illinois, Grant notified Frémont and, without waiting for his reply, advanced on [Paducah, Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paducah,_Kentucky "Paducah, Kentucky"), taking it without a fight on September 6.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFlood200563White2016159Bonekemper201221-108) Having understood the importance to Lincoln of Kentucky's neutrality, Grant assured its citizens, "I have come among you not as your enemy, but as your friend."[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198191Chernow2017153%E2%80%93155-109) On November 1, Frémont ordered Grant to "[make demonstrations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demonstration_(military) "Demonstration (military)")" against the Confederates on both sides of the Mississippi, but prohibited him from attacking.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016168-110)

### Belmont (1861), Forts Henry and Donelson (1862)

Main articles: [Battle of Belmont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Belmont "Battle of Belmont"), [Battle of Fort Henry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Fort_Henry "Battle of Fort Henry"), and [Battle of Fort Donelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Fort_Donelson "Battle of Fort Donelson")

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/%22Battle_of_Fort_Donelson.%22.jpg/250px-%22Battle_of_Fort_Donelson.%22.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:%22Battle_of_Fort_Donelson.%22.jpg)

_Battle of Fort Donelson_ by [Kurz and Allison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurz_and_Allison "Kurz and Allison"), 1887

On November 2, 1861, Lincoln removed Frémont from command, freeing Grant to attack Confederate soldiers encamped in [Cape Girardeau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Girardeau "Cape Girardeau"), Missouri.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016168-110) On November 5, Grant, along with Brigadier General [John A. McClernand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_A._McClernand "John A. McClernand"), landed 2,500 men at Hunter's Point, and on November 7 engaged the Confederates at the [Battle of Belmont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Belmont "Battle of Belmont").[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016169%E2%80%93171-111) The Union army took the camp, but the reinforced Confederates under Brigadier Generals [Frank Cheatham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Cheatham "Frank Cheatham") and [Gideon J. Pillow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gideon_J._Pillow "Gideon J. Pillow") forced a chaotic Union retreat.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016172-112) Grant had wanted to destroy Confederate strongholds at [Belmont, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belmont,_Missouri "Belmont, Missouri"), and [Columbus, Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus,_Kentucky "Columbus, Kentucky"), but was not given enough troops and was only able to disrupt their positions. Grant's troops escaped back to Cairo under fire from the fortified stronghold at Columbus.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016172%E2%80%93173Groom201294,_101%E2%80%93103-113) Although Grant and his army retreated, the battle gave his volunteers much-needed confidence and experience.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198192%E2%80%9394-114)

Columbus blocked Union access to the lower Mississippi. Grant and lieutenant colonel [James B. McPherson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_B._McPherson "James B. McPherson") planned to bypass Columbus and move against [Fort Henry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Fort_Henry "Battle of Fort Henry") on the [Tennessee River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee_River "Tennessee River"). They would then march east to [Fort Donelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Donelson "Fort Donelson") on the [Cumberland River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumberland_River "Cumberland River"), with the aid of gunboats, opening both rivers and allowing the Union access further south. Grant presented his plan to [Henry Halleck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Halleck "Henry Halleck"), his new commander in the newly created [Department of Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Missouri "Department of Missouri").[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016168McFeely198194-115) Halleck rebuffed Grant, believing he needed twice the number of troops. However, after consulting McClellan, he finally agreed on the condition that the attack would be in close cooperation with Navy flag officer [Andrew H. Foote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_H._Foote "Andrew H. Foote").[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001138%E2%80%93142Groom2012101%E2%80%93103-116) Foote's gunboats bombarded Fort Henry, leading to its surrender on February 6, 1862, before Grant's infantry even arrived.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001146-117)

Grant ordered an immediate [assault on Fort Donelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Fort_Donelson "Battle of Fort Donelson"), which dominated the Cumberland River. Unaware of the garrison's strength, Grant, McClernand, and Smith positioned their divisions around the fort. The next day McClernand and Smith independently launched probing attacks on apparent weak spots but were forced to retreat. On February 14, Foote's gunboats began bombarding the fort, only to be repulsed by its heavy guns. The next day, Pillow attacked and routed McClernand's division. Union reinforcements arrived, giving Grant a total force of over 40,000 men. Grant was with Foote four miles away when the Confederates attacked. Hearing the battle, Grant rode back and rallied his troop commanders, riding over seven miles of freezing roads and trenches, exchanging reports. When Grant blocked the Nashville Road, the Confederates retreated back into Fort Donelson.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAxelrod2011210-118) On February 16, Foote resumed his bombardment, signaling a general attack. Confederate generals [John B. Floyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_B._Floyd "John B. Floyd") and Pillow fled, leaving the fort in command of [Simon Bolivar Buckner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Bolivar_Buckner "Simon Bolivar Buckner"), who submitted to Grant's demand for "unconditional and immediate surrender".[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001141%E2%80%93164Brands2012a164%E2%80%93165-119)

Grant had won the first major victory for the Union, capturing Floyd's entire army of more than 12,000. Halleck was angry that Grant had acted without his authorization and complained to McClellan, accusing Grant of "neglect and inefficiency". On March 3, Halleck sent a telegram to Washington complaining that he had no communication with Grant for a week. Three days later, Halleck claimed "word has just reached me that... Grant has resumed his bad habits (of drinking)."[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGroom2012138,_143%E2%80%93144-120) Lincoln, regardless, promoted Grant to major general of volunteers and the Northern press treated Grant as a hero. Playing off his initials, they took to calling him "Unconditional Surrender Grant".[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012a164%E2%80%93165Smith2001125%E2%80%93134-121)

### Shiloh (1862) and aftermath

Further information: [Battle of Shiloh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Shiloh "Battle of Shiloh")

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c1/Thure_de_Thulstrup_-_Battle_of_Shiloh_%28cropped%29.jpg/330px-Thure_de_Thulstrup_-_Battle_of_Shiloh_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Thure_de_Thulstrup_-_Battle_of_Shiloh_(cropped).jpg)

_Battle of Shiloh_ by [Thure de Thulstrup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thure_de_Thulstrup "Thure de Thulstrup"), 1888

Reinstated by Halleck at the urging of Lincoln and Secretary of War [Edwin Stanton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Stanton "Edwin Stanton"), Grant rejoined his army with orders to advance with the [Army of the Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Army_of_the_Tennessee "Army of the Tennessee") into Tennessee. His main army was located at [Pittsburg Landing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburg_Landing "Pittsburg Landing"), while 40,000 Confederate troops converged at [Corinth, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corinth,_Mississippi "Corinth, Mississippi").[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016210Barney2011287-122) Grant wanted to attack the Confederates at Corinth, but Halleck ordered him not to attack until Major General [Don Carlos Buell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Carlos_Buell "Don Carlos Buell") arrived with his division of 25,000.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981111%E2%80%93112Groom201263White2016211-123) Grant prepared for an attack on the Confederate army of roughly equal strength. Instead of preparing defensive fortifications, they spent most of their time drilling the largely inexperienced troops while Sherman dismissed reports of nearby Confederates.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGroom201262%E2%80%9365McFeely1981112-124)

On the morning of April 6, 1862, Grant's troops were taken by surprise when the Confederates, led by Generals [Albert Sidney Johnston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Sidney_Johnston "Albert Sidney Johnston") and [P. G. T. Beauregard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P._G._T._Beauregard "P. G. T. Beauregard"), struck first "like an Alpine avalanche" near Shiloh church, attacking five divisions of Grant's army and forcing a confused retreat toward the Tennessee River.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981111Bonekemper201251,_94Barney2011287-125) Johnston was killed and command fell upon Beauregard.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016217%E2%80%93218-126) One Union line held the Confederate attack off for several hours, giving Grant time to assemble artillery and 20,000 troops near Pittsburg Landing.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBonekemper201251,_58%E2%80%9359,_63%E2%80%9364-127) The Confederates finally broke and captured a Union division, but Grant's newly assembled line held the landing, while the exhausted Confederates, lacking reinforcements, halted their advance.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981114Flood2005109,_112Bonekemper201251,_58%E2%80%9359,_63%E2%80%9364-128)[[g]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-130)

Bolstered by 18,000 troops from the divisions of Major Generals Buell and [Lew Wallace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lew_Wallace "Lew Wallace"), Grant counterattacked at dawn the next day and regained the field, forcing the disorganized and demoralized rebels to retreat to Corinth.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBonekemper201259,_63%E2%80%9364Smith2001206-131) Halleck ordered Grant not to advance more than one day's march from Pittsburg Landing, stopping the pursuit.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981115%E2%80%9316-132) Although Grant had won the battle, the situation was little changed.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981115-133) Grant, now realizing that the South was determined to fight, would later write, "Then, indeed, I gave up all idea of saving the Union except by complete conquest."[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012a187%E2%80%9388-134)

Shiloh was the costliest battle in American history to that point and the staggering 23,746 casualties stunned the nation.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBonekemper201294White2016221-135) Briefly hailed a hero for routing the Confederates, Grant was soon mired in controversy.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016223%E2%80%93224-136) The Northern press castigated Grant for shockingly high casualties, and accused him of drunkenness during the battle, contrary to the accounts of those with him at the time.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan20151109%E2%80%931119White2016223%E2%80%93225-137) Discouraged, Grant considered resigning but Sherman convinced him to stay.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012a188%E2%80%93191White2016230%E2%80%93231-138) Lincoln dismissed Grant's critics, saying "I can't spare this man; he fights."[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016225%E2%80%93226-139) Grant's costly victory at Shiloh ended any chance for the Confederates to prevail in the Mississippi valley or regain its strategic advantage in the West.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001204Barney2011289-140)

Halleck arrived from St. Louis on April 11, took command, and assembled a combined army of about 120,000 men. On April 29, he relieved Grant of field command and replaced him with Major General [George Henry Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Henry_Thomas "George Henry Thomas"). Halleck slowly marched his army to take Corinth, entrenching each night.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016229-141) Meanwhile, Beauregard pretended to be reinforcing, sent "deserters" to the Union Army with that story, and moved his army out during the night, to Halleck's surprise when he finally [arrived at Corinth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Battle_of_Corinth "First Battle of Corinth") on May 30.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016230Groom2012363%E2%80%93364-142)

Halleck divided his combined army and reinstated Grant as field commander on July 11.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTELongacre2006137White2016231-143) Later that year, on September 19, Grant's army defeated Confederates at the [Battle of Iuka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Iuka "Battle of Iuka"), then successfully [defended Corinth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Battle_of_Corinth "Second Battle of Corinth"), inflicting heavy casualties.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012a211%E2%80%93212-144) On October 25, Grant assumed command of the District of the Tennessee.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBadeau1971126-145) In November, after Lincoln's preliminary [Emancipation Proclamation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emancipation_Proclamation "Emancipation Proclamation"), Grant ordered units under his command to incorporate former slaves into the Union Army, giving them clothes, shelter, and wages for their services.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFlood2005133-146)

### Vicksburg campaign (1862–1863)

Further information: [Vicksburg campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicksburg_campaign "Vicksburg campaign") and [General Order No. 11 (1862)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Order_No._11_(1862) "General Order No. 11 (1862)")

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b9/VicksburgBlockade.jpg/330px-VicksburgBlockade.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:VicksburgBlockade.jpg)

Grant's successful gamble: Porter's gunboats night ran the Confederate gauntlet at Vicksburg on the [Mississippi River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River "Mississippi River").

The Union capture of [Vicksburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicksburg,_Mississippi "Vicksburg, Mississippi"), the last Confederate stronghold on the [Mississippi River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River "Mississippi River"), was considered vital as it would split the Confederacy in two.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016243Miller2019xiiChernow2017236-147) Lincoln appointed McClernand for the job, rather than Grant or Sherman.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012a221%E2%80%93223Catton2005112Chernow2017236%E2%80%93237-148) Halleck, who retained power over troop displacement, ordered McClernand to [Memphis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memphis,_Tennessee "Memphis, Tennessee"), and placed him and his troops under Grant's authority.[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFlood2005147%E2%80%93148White2016246Chernow2017238%E2%80%93239-149)

On November 13, 1862, Grant captured [Holly Springs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holly_Springs,_Mississippi "Holly Springs, Mississippi") and advanced to [Corinth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corinth,_Mississippi "Corinth, Mississippi").[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016248Chernow2017231%E2%80%93232-150) His plan was to attack Vicksburg overland, while Sherman would attack Vicksburg from Chickasaw Bayou.[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017239-151) However, Confederate cavalry raids on December 11 and 20 broke Union communications and recaptured Holly Springs, preventing Grant and Sherman from converging on Vicksburg.[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatton2005119,_291White2016248%E2%80%93249Chernow2017239%E2%80%93241-152) The most significant of these raids was led by Confederate General [Earl Van Dorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_Van_Dorn "Earl Van Dorn"), whose successful surprise attack at [Holly Springs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holly_Springs_Raid "Holly Springs Raid") on December 20, 1862, destroyed Grant's supply base and forced him to abandon his overland advance on Vicksburg.[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001244-153) McClernand reached Sherman's army, assumed command, and independently of Grant led a campaign that captured Confederate [Fort Hindman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Arkansas_Post_(1863) "Battle of Arkansas Post (1863)").[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBonekemper2012147%E2%80%93148-154) After the sack of Holly Springs, Grant considered and sometimes adopted the strategy of foraging the land,[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller2019248-155) rather than exposing long Union supply lines to enemy attack.[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001244-153)

Fugitive [African-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African-American "African-American") slaves poured into Grant's district, whom he sent north to Cairo to be domestic servants in Chicago. However, Lincoln ended this when Illinois political leaders complained.[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller2019206%E2%80%93207-156) On his own initiative, Grant set up a pragmatic program and hired Presbyterian chaplain [John Eaton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Eaton_(general) "John Eaton (general)") to administer [contraband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contraband_(American_Civil_War) "Contraband (American Civil War)") camps.[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller2019206%E2%80%93209-157) Freed slaves picked cotton that was shipped north to aid the Union war effort. Lincoln approved and Grant's program was successful.[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller2019209%E2%80%93210-158) Grant also worked freed black labor on [a canal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grant's_Canal "Grant's Canal") to bypass Vicksburg, incorporating the laborers into the Union Army and Navy.[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016Miller2019154%E2%80%93155-159)

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/37/Battle_of_Jackson_%28cropped%29.tif/lossy-page1-330px-Battle_of_Jackson_%28cropped%29.tif.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Battle_of_Jackson_(cropped).tif)

The [Battle of Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Jackson,_Mississippi "Battle of Jackson, Mississippi"), fought on May 14, 1863, was part of the [Vicksburg campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicksburg_campaign "Vicksburg campaign").

Grant's war responsibilities included combating illegal Northern cotton trade and civilian obstruction.[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001225White2016235%E2%80%9336-160)[[h]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-163) He had received numerous complaints about Jewish speculators in his district.[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller2019259-164) The majority, however, of those involved in illegal trading were not Jewish.[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017232%E2%80%9333Howland1868123%E2%80%9324-165) To help combat this, Grant required two permits, one from the Treasury and one from the Union Army, to purchase cotton.[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017232-161) On December 17, 1862, Grant issued a controversial [General Order No. 11](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Order_No._11_(1862) "General Order No. 11 (1862)"), expelling "Jews, as a class", from his military district.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012a218Shevitz2005256-166) After complaints, Lincoln rescinded th

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

(Redirected from [List of presidents of the United States by cause of death](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_cause_of_death&redirect=no "List of presidents of the United States by cause of death"))

Of the 45 people who have served as [President of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") since the office came into existence in 1789,[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_cause_of_death#cite_note-1) 40 have died–eight of them while [in office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incumbent "Incumbent").[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_cause_of_death#cite_note-2)

The [oldest president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_age "List of presidents of the United States by age") at the time of death was [Jimmy Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter "Jimmy Carter"), who died at 100 years, 89 days. [John F. Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy "John F. Kennedy"), [assassinated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_John_F._Kennedy "Assassination of John F. Kennedy") at the age of 46 years, 177 days, was the youngest to have died in office; the youngest to have [died by natural causes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_by_natural_causes "Death by natural causes") was [James K. Polk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_K._Polk "James K. Polk"), who died of [cholera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cholera "Cholera") at the age of 53 years, 225 days.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

(Redirected from [List of presidents of the United States by cause of death](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_cause_of_death&redirect=no "List of presidents of the United States by cause of death"))

Of the 45 people who have served as [President of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") since the office came into existence in 1789,[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_cause_of_death#cite_note-1) 40 have died–eight of them while [in office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incumbent "Incumbent").[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_cause_of_death#cite_note-2)

The [oldest president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_age "List of presidents of the United States by age") at the time of death was [Jimmy Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter "Jimmy Carter"), who died at 100 years, 89 days. [John F. Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy "John F. Kennedy"), [assassinated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_John_F._Kennedy "Assassination of John F. Kennedy") at the age of 46 years, 177 days, was the youngest to have died in office; the youngest to have [died by natural causes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_by_natural_causes "Death by natural causes") was [James K. Polk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_K._Polk "James K. Polk"), who died of [cholera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cholera "Cholera") at the age of 53 years, 225 days.

Of the 45 people who have served as [President of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") since the office came into existence in 1789,[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_cause_of_death&printable=yes#cite_note-1) 40 have died–eight of them while [in office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incumbent "Incumbent").[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_cause_of_death&printable=yes#cite_note-2)

The [oldest president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_age "List of presidents of the United States by age") at the time of death was [Jimmy Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter "Jimmy Carter"), who died at 100 years, 89 days. [John F. Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy "John F. Kennedy"), [assassinated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_John_F._Kennedy "Assassination of John F. Kennedy") at the age of 46 years, 177 days, was the youngest to have died in office; the youngest to have [died by natural causes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_by_natural_causes "Death by natural causes") was [James K. Polk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_K._Polk "James K. Polk"), who died of [cholera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cholera "Cholera") at the age of 53 years, 225 days.

### Same day

*   July 4, 1826: [Thomas Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson "Thomas Jefferson") at 12:50 p.m.,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_cause_of_death&printable=yes#cite_note-US_Pres-22) and [John Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Adams "John Adams") at 6:20 p.m.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_cause_of_death&printable=yes#cite_note-US_Pres-22)

### Same date

*   March 8: [Millard Fillmore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millard_Fillmore "Millard Fillmore") in 1874 and [William Howard Taft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Howard_Taft "William Howard Taft") in 1930
*   July 4: [John Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Adams "John Adams") and [Thomas Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson "Thomas Jefferson") in 1826, and [James Monroe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Monroe "James Monroe") in 1831[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_cause_of_death&printable=yes#cite_note-23)
*   December 26: [Harry S. Truman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman "Harry S. Truman") in 1972 and [Gerald Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_Ford "Gerald Ford") in 2006

### Same calendar year

*   1826: [Thomas Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson "Thomas Jefferson") and [John Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Adams "John Adams") on July 4
*   1862: [John Tyler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Tyler "John Tyler") and [Martin Van Buren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren "Martin Van Buren"), on January 18 and July 24, respectively

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

(Redirected from [List of presidents of the United States by cause of death](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_cause_of_death&redirect=no "List of presidents of the United States by cause of death"))

The printable version is no longer supported and may have rendering errors. Please update your browser bookmarks and please use the default browser print function instead.

Of the 45 people who have served as [President of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") since the office came into existence in 1789,[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_cause_of_death&printable=yes#cite_note-1) 40 have died–eight of them while [in office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incumbent "Incumbent").[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_cause_of_death&printable=yes#cite_note-2)

The [oldest president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_age "List of presidents of the United States by age") at the time of death was [Jimmy Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter "Jimmy Carter"), who died at 100 years, 89 days. [John F. Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy "John F. Kennedy"), [assassinated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_John_F._Kennedy "Assassination of John F. Kennedy") at the age of 46 years, 177 days, was the youngest to have died in office; the youngest to have [died by natural causes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_by_natural_causes "Death by natural causes") was [James K. Polk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_K._Polk "James K. Polk"), who died of [cholera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cholera "Cholera") at the age of 53 years, 225 days.

## Died same day, date, year, age

### Same day

*   July 4, 1826: [Thomas Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson "Thomas Jefferson") at 12:50 p.m.,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_cause_of_death&printable=yes#cite_note-US_Pres-22) and [John Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Adams "John Adams") at 6:20 p.m.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_cause_of_death&printable=yes#cite_note-US_Pres-22)

### Same date

*   March 8: [Millard Fillmore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millard_Fillmore "Millard Fillmore") in 1874 and [William Howard Taft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Howard_Taft "William Howard Taft") in 1930
*   July 4: [John Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Adams "John Adams") and [Thomas Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson "Thomas Jefferson") in 1826, and [James Monroe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Monroe "James Monroe") in 1831[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_cause_of_death&printable=yes#cite_note-23)
*   December 26: [Harry S. Truman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman "Harry S. Truman") in 1972 and [Gerald Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_Ford "Gerald Ford") in 2006

### Same calendar year

*   1826: [Thomas Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson "Thomas Jefferson") and [John Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Adams "John Adams") on July 4
*   1862: [John Tyler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Tyler "John Tyler") and [Martin Van Buren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Van_Buren "Martin Van Buren"), on January 18 and July 24, respectively
*   1901: [Benjamin Harrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Harrison "Benjamin Harrison") and [William McKinley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_McKinley "William McKinley"), on March 13 and September 14, respectively

### Same age (rounded down to nearest year)

*   93: [Gerald Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_Ford "Gerald Ford") and [Ronald Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan "Ronald Reagan")
*   90: [John Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Adams "John Adams") and [Herbert Hoover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Hoover "Herbert Hoover")
*   78: [Andrew Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Jackson "Andrew Jackson") and [Dwight D. Eisenhower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dwight_D._Eisenhower "Dwight D. Eisenhower")
*   71: [John Tyler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Tyler "John Tyler") and Grover Cleveland
*   67: [George Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington "George Washington"), [Benjamin Harrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Harrison "Benjamin Harrison"), and [Woodrow Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodrow_Wilson "Woodrow Wilson")
*   64: [Franklin Pierce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_Pierce "Franklin Pierce") and [Lyndon B. Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyndon_B._Johnson "Lyndon B. Johnson")
*   63: Ulysses S. Grant and [Franklin D. Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt "Franklin D. Roosevelt")
*   60: [Theodore Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_Roosevelt "Theodore Roosevelt") and [Calvin Coolidge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvin_Coolidge "Calvin Coolidge")
*   57: [Chester A. Arthur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chester_A._Arthur "Chester A. Arthur") and [Warren G. Harding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_G._Harding "Warren G. Harding")
